content: Dock10, also referred to as Zizimin3, is a large intracellular protein with a molecular weight of approximately 240 kDa. It plays a role in intracellular signaling pathways. Dock10 belongs to the DOCK-D subfamily within the DOCK family of guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs), which are known to activate small G proteins. Dock10 was discovered through bioinformatics approaches as part of a family of evolutionarily conserved proteins, the DOCK family, which share significant sequence homology. It is expressed in peripheral blood leukocytes as well as in the brain, spleen, lung, and thymus. Structurally, Dock10 shares the same domain arrangement and a high degree of sequence similarity with other members of the DOCK-D/Zizimin subfamily. It contains a DHR-2 domain, which is involved in binding small G proteins, and a DHR-1 domain, which in some DOCK family proteins interacts with membrane phospholipids. Additionally, Dock10, like other DOCK-D subfamily proteins, has an N-terminal PH domain. In Dock9/Zizimin1, this domain facilitates recruitment to the plasma membrane. The DHR-2 domain of Dock10 has been shown to bind small G proteins such as Cdc42, TC10, and TCL, although these interactions are characterized by low affinity. The physiological role of Dock10 remains poorly understood. However, research in lymphocytes has demonstrated that Dock10 expression is upregulated in B-lymphocytes and Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) cells in response to the cytokine IL-4. This finding suggests that Dock10 may play a role in B-cell activation and proliferation. Another study identified Dock10 as a protein that is overexpressed in certain aggressive papillary thyroid carcinomas, indicating a potential involvement in tumorigenesis.
